power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Search for the definition of a fixed mindset today and you'll likely encounter a single theory presented as settled fact: Carol Dweck's definition.
You might even hear that Dweck coined the phrase in 2006.
Yet a broader history tells a different story.
The earliest identified description comes from intelligence analyst Richards Heuer in 1981, while the idea has roots that stretch back even further.
This invites an interesting inquiry: for a field that talks so much about growth, how much of a learn-it-all attitude have we brought to our understanding of fixed mindset?
Perhaps one of the most interesting tests of a growth mindset is what we do when we discover that the story we thought we knew is not the whole story.
This perspectives paper explores this broader history of fixed mindset and asks: Who gets to decide what a fixed mindset is?
Has an entire generation of people inherited a fixed idea of what fixed mindset means?
And what might become possible if we learn from a broader range of perspectives, including our own lived experiences?
Here is a test you can try for yourself right now.
Type "What is a fixed mindset?"
into a search engine or an AI chatbot.
Notice what comes back.
If you're feeling extra studious, you might also like to consult the peer-reviewed literature or a psychology textbook.
Done?
What did you find?
Despite searching in many different places, you likely encountered the same confident answer, sometimes presented as settled fact: Stanford professor Carol Dweck's theory.
This is the idea that a fixed mindset is a belief that intelligence and ability cannot be developed (Dweck, 2006).
text.formatted: This is the idea that a fixed mindset is a belief that intelligence and ability cannot be developed <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dweck, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In some cases, you may even find Dweck is credited with coining the phrase itself.
At first glance, there may seem to be little reason to question this answer.
It is repeated so widely and confidently across so many mediums that it can appear like it is the whole story.
Look a little deeper, however, and a different story begins to emerge, one that is older, richer, and more diverse than the popular account suggests.
Who am I and why did I decide to write this perspectives paper?
I am a mindset scholar who was initially taught that fixed and growth mindset theory was the legitimate foundation for research in the mindset field.

Over time, I came to learn that fixed and growth mindset was one theory of many, and that there is a larger field of mindset science that stretches back over 100 years (e.g., Bolton, 1909; Buchanan, 2023 Buchanan, , 2024;; Crum & Langer, 2007; Fisher, 1988; French, 2016; Kegan & Lahey, 2009; Kilpatrick, 1925).
text.formatted: Over time, I came to learn that fixed and growth mindset was one theory of many, and that there is a larger field of mindset science that stretches back over 100 years (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Bolton, 1909;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Buchanan, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Buchanan, , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crum & Langer, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Fisher, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">French, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Kegan & Lahey, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kilpatrick, 1925)</ref>.

text.text: When I looked into the origins of fixed mindset, I discovered an often-overlooked history that was both amazing and humbling.
It helped me expand my understanding, and made me realise that at times, I had been approaching fixed mindset with a fixed mindset of my own.
This paper shares the larger story that emerged from that inquiry.
We'll begin by exploring a largely overlooked history of fixed mindset, including diverse perspectives that emerged decades before the theory that most of us know today.
We will then look across these perspectives and ask what each of them might have to teach us, and what we risk missing if one theory becomes the socially accepted default.
Most of all, you are invited to approach fixed mindset with a learn-it-all attitude, and explore how your own understanding may want to grow.
To be clear, the purpose of this examination is not to dismiss the value of Dweck's theory.
It has achieved global popularity for a reason: it offers a simple, easy to understand framework.
A core question here is to examine the implications if it has become the sole theory of a fixed mindset.
And what might become possible if we embraced broader perspectives, including our own.
This historical search used Google Scholar and Google Search to find publications that used the phrases "fixed mindset", "fixed mind-set", and "fixed-mind set" between 1900 and 2006.
The publications included books, research papers, and conference proceedings.
Each usage was then reviewed to see if it provided what might reasonably be interpreted as a description or definition of a fixed mindset.
Seven distinct uses met this criterion and were included in the historical exploration that follows.
A second search looked for adjacent concepts that didn't use the phrase fixed mindset, but offered a definition or description related to how a mindset can become fixed or set.
This search yielded three additional concepts for consideration.
The purpose of these historical searches was not to conduct an exhaustive or systematic review of every use of fixed mindset.
Rather, it was to identify historical examples that could help test the commonly presented story that fixed mindset began with Dweck in 2006, and to explore what prior perspectives might teach us.
text.formatted: Rather, it was to identify historical examples that could help test the commonly presented story that fixed mindset began with <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Dweck in 2006, and to</ref> explore what prior perspectives might teach us.

text.text: The identified perspectives were then reviewed alongside one another to examine what they reveal.
As such, the ten examples presented here should not be read as a complete history of fixed mindset.
Other relevant uses and concepts may exist, and future research could build on this exploratory work through a more systematic review of the literature.
The earliest description identified in this review comes from intelligence analyst Richards Heuer.

In 1981, Heuer described a fixed mindset as a tendency to fit new information into an existing system of beliefs, and to evaluate data solely in the context of a single hypothesis already believed to be most likely.
His proposed intervention to address a fixed mindset was to adopt a point of view associated with multiple hypotheses, not just the favoured one (Heuer, 1981).
text.formatted: His proposed intervention to address a fixed mindset was to adopt a point of view associated with multiple hypotheses, not just the favoured one <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Heuer, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: In Heuer's words: [We] all have a tendency to develop a fixed mindset and then to fit new information into this existing system of beliefs.

We often evaluate new information in the context of the single hypothesis which we already believe to be most likely. (Heuer, 1981, p. 106) In 1985, Professor Shozo Hibino used the phrase "fixed-mind" set in the context of participatory planning and design.
text.formatted: We often evaluate new information in the context of the single hypothesis which we already believe to be most likely. <ref type="bibr">(Heuer, 1981, p. 106)</ref> In 1985, Professor Shozo Hibino used the phrase "fixed-mind" set in the context of participatory planning and design.

text.text: Hibino did not provide a formal definition, but associated a fixed-mind set with becoming stuck when attempting to solve a problem.
His proposed response was to broaden one's purpose and view the problem from a wider perspective (Hibino, 1985).
text.formatted: His proposed response was to broaden one's purpose and view the problem from a wider perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hibino, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: In 1993, Timothy Ingalsbee used fixed mindset in social psychology to describe rigid and monolithic ideological beliefs, values, and goals.
He contrasted a fixed mindset with the more diverse and dynamic mindsets of collective action networks (Ingalsbee, 1993).
text.formatted: He contrasted a fixed mindset with the more diverse and dynamic mindsets of collective action networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Ingalsbee, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: A year later, in 1994, David Cowan used fixed mind-set to describe a narrow focus in brand marketing.

Cowan described managers becoming overly fixed on particular measures of performance, limiting their ability to recognise broader sales opportunities or strategies that could benefit an entire product line (Cowan, 1994).
text.formatted: Cowan described managers becoming overly fixed on particular measures of performance, limiting their ability to recognise broader sales opportunities or strategies that could benefit an entire product line <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cowan, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: In 1997, Sui Pheng Low and Hennie Faizathy Omar brought another meaning to the phrase.
They associated a fixed mindset with a conservative attitude that avoids innovation in quality management.
They argued that such an orientation could make it difficult for organisations to maintain the dynamism needed to adapt in rapidly changing environments (Pheng Low & Faizathy Omar, 1997).
text.formatted: They argued that such an orientation could make it difficult for organisations to maintain the dynamism needed to adapt in rapidly changing environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Pheng Low & Faizathy Omar, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: In 2000, Mabila Mathebula offered perhaps the most vivid image of fixed mindset in this early history.
Writing about the railway industry, Mathebula associated fixed mindset with fixed plans and old paradigms.
He compared this way of working with travelling along a railway line, where movement is confined to predetermined tracks, stations, and timetables (Mathebula, 2000).
text.formatted: He compared this way of working with travelling along a railway line, where movement is confined to predetermined tracks, stations, and timetables <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Mathebula, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: As Mathebula writes:
With railroads, people could travel only between fixed points on the same track, based on a dictated timetable.

The fixed plans, fixed rail, fixed stations and the fixed time schedule created a fixed mindset among railway employees and management. (Mathebula, 2000, p. 1) Finally, in 2006, Professor Carol Dweck introduced the definition of fixed mindset that would eventually become the most popular: a belief that qualities such as intelligence and ability are fixed rather than developable (Dweck, 2006).
text.formatted: The fixed plans, fixed rail, fixed stations and the fixed time schedule created a fixed mindset among railway employees and management. <ref type="bibr">(Mathebula, 2000, p. 1)</ref> Finally, in 2006, Professor Carol Dweck introduced the definition of fixed mindset that would eventually become the most popular: a belief that qualities such as intelligence and ability are fixed rather than developable <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dweck, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: This definition also has its own longer history.
For decades, Dweck and her colleagues had studied what they called entity and incremental theories.
However, they faced a challenge that nobody could remember "entity" and "incremental".
So, a decision was made to rename "entity" to "fixed mindset" in 2006 (Dweck & Yeager, 2019).
text.formatted: So, a decision was made to rename "entity" to "fixed mindset" in 2006 <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dweck & Yeager, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This means the definition of fixed mindset many of us know well today has its roots in entity research.
To shift out of a fixed mindset, Dweck proposes cultivating a growth mindset: a belief that human qualities can be developed.
As far as this review could discern, these uses of fixed mindset appear to have arisen at different times and in different contexts, with similar yet distinct meanings.
Indeed, both their similarities and differences are part of what makes this history so interesting.
Across different fields, the same phrase was used to make sense of different ways that a mindset can become fixed.
This history becomes even more interesting when we examine adjacent ideas that didn't use the phrase fixed mindset, but did study related ways in which a mindset can become fixed or set.
One of the earliest examples identified comes from educator Ira Meyers.
In 1908, Meyers shared the following passage, which explores how accepted dogma or statement can cause a mind to become set, and how broad-sense experience can help create possibilities for growth.

"One result of broad-sense experience is to retain plasticity in mental attitude; if the mental attitude of the individual evolves out of his own experiences it will remain plastic and keep in adjustment and harmony with increase in experience; if however, it is the product of accepted dogma or statement, something based on a statement of authority, teacher, or text-book, the mind becomes set and excludes all possibility for growth in that direction." (Meyers, 1908, p. 317) In 1942, Abraham Luchins studied the Einstellung effect, and what he called mechanisation in problem solving.
text.formatted: "One result of broad-sense experience is to retain plasticity in mental attitude; if the mental attitude of the individual evolves out of his own experiences it will remain plastic and keep in adjustment and harmony with increase in experience; if however, it is the product of accepted dogma or statement, something based on a statement of authority, teacher, or text-book, the mind becomes set and excludes all possibility for growth in that direction." <ref type="bibr">(Meyers, 1908, p. 317)</ref> In 1942, Abraham Luchins studied the Einstellung effect, and what he called mechanisation in problem solving.

text.text: His work explored how a solution that has worked in the past can become the solution people continue to use in the future, even when alternative or more appropriate solutions are available (Luchins, 1942).
text.formatted: His work explored how a solution that has worked in the past can become the solution people continue to use in the future, even when alternative or more appropriate solutions are available <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Luchins, 1942)</ref>.

text.text: In this case, what becomes fixed is a person's Einstellung (a German term meaning attitude or set) and, with it, their approach to a task or problem.
A related idea appears in Karl Duncker's work in 1945 on functional fixedness (Funktionsgebundenheit).
Duncker explored how a person's existing set or Einstellung can limit what they are able to see.
People may fail to recognise novel uses for familiar objects because restructuring an established set or Einstellung can be difficult (Duncker, 1945).
text.formatted: People may fail to recognise novel uses for familiar objects because restructuring an established set or Einstellung can be difficult <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Duncker, 1945)</ref>.

text.text: Placing these ideas alongside the history of fixed mindset helps us to see that there may be much to learn from adjacent ideas and bodies of work.
What Then, is a Fixed Mindset?
Perhaps the simplest finding here is that there is more than one way to understand a fixed mindset, and that different people have interpreted it in different ways.
For Heuer (1981), a fixed mindset involves becoming fixed on a single hypothesis and fitting new information into an existing system of beliefs.
text.formatted: For <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Heuer (1981)</ref>, a fixed mindset involves becoming fixed on a single hypothesis and fitting new information into an existing system of beliefs.

text.text: For Ingalsbee (1993), it involves rigid beliefs, values, and goals.
text.formatted: For <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Ingalsbee (1993)</ref>, it involves rigid beliefs, values, and goals.

text.text: For Mathebula (2000), it is associated with fixed plans and old paradigms.
text.formatted: For <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Mathebula (2000)</ref>, it is associated with fixed plans and old paradigms.

text.text: For Dweck (2006), it is believing that qualities such as intelligence and ability are fixed rather than developable.
text.formatted: For <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Dweck (2006)</ref>, it is believing that qualities such as intelligence and ability are fixed rather than developable.

text.text: And if we look beyond the phrase itself, ideas such as the Einstellung effect and functional fixedness offer still more ways of understanding how our mindset can become fixed (Luchins, 1942; Duncker, 1945).
text.formatted: And if we look beyond the phrase itself, ideas such as the Einstellung effect and functional fixedness offer still more ways of understanding how our mindset can become fixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Luchins, 1942;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Duncker, 1945)</ref>.

text.text: There is an interesting irony at play here.
Heuer warned that a fixed mindset can develop when we become attached to a single hypothesis and fit new information into what we already believe.

Meyers likewise warned that accepted dogma or statement, particularly based on a statement of authority, teacher, or textbook, can cause our minds to become set, and exclude all possibility for growth.
Seen in this light, perhaps the greatest irony in mindset theory is that our understanding of fixed mindset itself may have become fixed.

In turn, if textbooks, peer-reviewed papers, search results, and AI chatbot answers routinely present a single, monolithic definition of fixed mindset, might they be inadvertently reinforcing a fixed mindset about fixed mindset itself?
If they have, what might we need to change now to address these systems?
Do mindset textbooks need rewriting?
Do peer-review processes invite rethinking?
Do search algorithms require reindexing?
And do large language models welcome retraining to reflect more of a learn-it-all attitude?
 What are the implications if a single hypothesis of fixed mindset is shared all over the world?
 Who benefits when one theory of fixed mindset becomes the dominant account?
 How do our own lived experiences of a fixed mindset fit into the picture?
These questions become particularly important when we consider the role of our own lived experience.

If a fixed mindset is something that shows up in our own lives, how much say This experience makes me wonder about all the children in schools and adults in professional learning programs who are taught that a fixed mindset means believing human qualities cannot be developed, and that's it.
And what happens when millions of people turn to search engines and AI chatbots to ask what a fixed mindset is, only to be presented with a single, monolithic definition.
As more of us turn to search engines and AI to help us understand ideas like fixed mindset, which perspectives these systems make visible, and which they leave out, may increasingly matter.
If one perspective is all people encounter, are these systems helping people understand their own experience, or are they deciding in advance what other people's experience is supposed to mean?
Perhaps there is an opportunity here to put more power in people's hands.
Rather than pre-defining what a fixed mindset means, we could invite people to explore diverse perspectives alongside their own lived experience.
In doing so, people can play a more active role in constructing their own understanding of what a fixed mindset means in their own lives.
One response to the diverse perspectives presented here might be to point to construct validity.
Put simply, construct validity is the extent to which a theory or test accurately measures the abstract theoretical concept it claims to measure (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955).
text.formatted: Put simply, construct validity is the extent to which a theory or test accurately measures the abstract theoretical concept it claims to measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Cronbach & Meehl, 1955)</ref>.

text.text: Dweck and her colleagues have spent decades developing and testing entity theory (e.g., Dweck et al., 1995), while many of the other perspectives explored in this paper have not undergone the same degree of empirical scrutiny.
text.formatted: Dweck and her colleagues have spent decades developing and testing entity theory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dweck et al., 1995)</ref>, while many of the other perspectives explored in this paper have not undergone the same degree of empirical scrutiny.

text.text: It could therefore be argued that there are good scientific reasons for taking Dweck's theory seriously, while treating other ways of understanding or experiencing a fixed mindset with greater caution.
But there is an important distinction here.
Dweck's construct was originally validated to measure a range of very specific variables that relate to entity beliefs (e.g., Dweck et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Dweck's construct was originally validated to measure a range of very specific variables that relate to entity beliefs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dweck et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: It was later renamed to fixed mindset in 2006, to help make the construct more user-friendly (Dweck & Yeager, 2019).
text.formatted: It was later renamed to fixed mindset in 2006, to help make the construct more user-friendly <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dweck & Yeager, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This history matters.
Showing that a construct successfully measures entity beliefs is not necessarily the same thing as showing that it captures everything people might experience as a fixed mindset.

The risk here is that, over time, a construct that was originally developed to assess entity beliefs (one map) becomes treated as though it defines the entire phenomenon of fixed mindset (the whole territory).
For this reason, it is important not to conflate a construct that was originally designed to measure a specialised set of beliefs with the full range of ways people may understand a fixed mindset.
What's more, this review looked for large-scale research that asked people from diverse contexts how they actually experience a fixed mindset, but was unable to find such a study.
Instead, much of the literature reviewed here appears to begin with the assumption that fixed mindset is an entity belief and then investigates it on that basis (e.g., Dweck & Yeager, 2019).
text.formatted: Instead, much of the literature reviewed here appears to begin with the assumption that fixed mindset is an entity belief and then investigates it on that basis (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dweck & Yeager, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The possibility that fixed mindset may be experienced or understood in different ways appears to have received comparatively little attention.
This points to a dual opportunity for the future of fixed mindset theory.

On an empirical research level, there may be value in developing and testing a broader theoretical construct of fixed mindset, one that begins by listening to diverse lived experiences rather than deciding in advance what the phenomenon is.
Importantly, the answer to a fixed construct of fixed mindset is not to replace it with yet another fixed construct.
It is to develop a construct that is never set, but always growing.
On a personal level, people can also engage in their own action research by exploring how a fixed mindset actually shows up in their lives.
They can draw on different theories and perspectives, compare them with their own experience, and gradually construct a personalised map that better fits the territory of their lived reality.
In this approach, understanding is not something research establishes in advance and then is universally applied to everyone.

Rather, each person takes an active role in developing their own understanding by engaging with different perspectives, testing those perspectives against their own experience, and refining what a fixed mindset means to them over time.

An empirically validated construct can therefore be treated as one potentially valuable map without automatically being treated as the only legitimate map, or as more important than the understanding people develop through careful inquiry into their own lived experience.
To help all of this land, consider a 9-year-old child struggling with a maths assignment.
Their teacher sits beside them and asks how they are going.
The child says, "I'm no good at maths."
The teacher looks at them kindly and adds one word: "yet."
"You're not good at maths… yet."
The teacher then explains that, to overcome a fixed mindset, they need to believe in their ability to grow.
Now imagine the same situation unfolding differently.
This time, rather than arriving with an explanation, the teacher becomes curious.
They ask what is going on for the child and help them explore the experience in their own words.
Perhaps it does involve beliefs about intelligence and ability.
Perhaps it reflects one of the other forms of fixed mindset explored in this paper.
Or perhaps it has nothing to do with fixed mindset at all.
The teacher does not decide in advance.
They listen, learn, and update their understanding and beliefs as they go.
Here lies the irony.
The first teacher might appear to be teaching a growth mindset, but it might actually be that they are role-modelling a fixed mindset about fixed mindset.
Their mind is already set on what the problem is and they move to solve it with a standardised script.
The second teacher, in contrast, models more of a learning attitude.

Rather than fitting the child into an existing system of beliefs, they remain open, curious, and sensitive to context, allowing understanding to emerge through exploration of the child's lived experience.
In summary, this perspectives paper found that the history of fixed mindset is older and more diverse than the story that is commonly told.
Carol Dweck's 2006 theory of a fixed mindset is one valuable perspective among many, rather than the definitive origin or entire scope of the concept.
The paper also invites caution when any single, monolithic theory is presented as settled fact, as doing so may inadvertently encourage a fixed mindset about fixed mindset itself.
Rather than searching for the one "right" theory of fixed mindset, you may find it more useful to view each perspective as offering a different lens.
The more lenses you look through, the richer and more complete your understanding becomes.

Gets to Decide?
This brings us to some of the core questions that emerged from this research, and are offered to the wider field of mindset science for consideration: Who gets to decide what is a fixed mindset?
 Has an entire generation of people inherited a fixed idea of what fixed mindset means?
should we have in understanding what that experience means?
Speaking from my own experience, I have found the entity theory definition of fixed mindset to be quite limiting.
It captures something valuable, but it doesn't capture everything I would describe as a fixed mindset.
Learning about the perspectives of Heuer, Meyers, Mathebula, and others has helped me expand how I understand the different ways a fixed mindset can show up in my own life.
